title: Airport & Flight
strapline: Check in the cases, take your boarding pass, and fly off somewhere you've dreamed of.
intent: Children play out a big, exciting journey with a clear sequence — check in, security, boarding, take-off, landing — and hold the order in their heads.
Children draw on real experiences and imagined ones, telling everyone where they are flying and what they will see there.
Children mark-make with real purpose — boarding passes, luggage tags, passports and a departures board that the play depends on.
Children weigh, count and compare — heavy cases, seat numbers, how many minutes until take-off.
Children discover that the wider world is full of different places, languages and journeys — and that flying connects them.
implementation: Set up stations in order — a check-in desk, a security arch, a row of chairs as the cabin — so the sequence is built into the space.
Take a passenger role and follow the children's rules: hand over your case, ask where the gate is, buckle up when told.
Model the journey talk: 'Flight to Jamaica now boarding at gate three — please have your passports ready.'
Bring in the maths honestly — weigh the cases on real scales, count the seats, find seat number 4.
Provide passports, tickets and luggage tags to write, and let children invent the destinations.
Add a map or globe and talk about where families have flown, and the languages spoken there.
Let a captain make announcements and a cabin crew serve the drinks, so everyone has a job.
key_questions: Where is your flight going today, and what will you pack?
This case feels heavy — shall we weigh it? Which is heaviest?
What do we need to write on the boarding pass so you get the right seat?
What happens first at the airport, and what comes next?
How many minutes until take-off — shall we count them down?

impact.text: Children play out the airport sequence in order — check in, security, board, fly, land — and keep the storyline going with others.
Children tell everyone where they are flying and recount real or imagined journeys in rough sequence.
Children write boarding passes, luggage tags and passports — marks that carry a real message.
Children weigh cases and compare heavier and lighter using real number talk.
Children count seats and find seat numbers, matching a passenger to each place.
Children talk about far-off places, other languages and the families who travel to them, and find that different is interesting.
Children take on roles — captain, crew, passenger — and cooperate to keep the flight running.

enhancements: A check-in desk with scales, a stamp, luggage tags and a queue rope.
Blank passports, boarding passes and a departures board to fill in and rub out.
A row of chairs with seatbelts (scarves) and a captain's cap for announcements.
Small wheeled cases and dressing-up for the journey somewhere hot or cold.
A world map or globe marking where children's families have travelled.
A trolley of pretend snacks and drinks for the cabin crew to serve.
Headphones, a walkie-talkie and a control-tower window for landing the planes.

playing_exploring: Children pour their real trips and their wildest wishes into where the plane is going.
They test the airport's rules by playing them — what if my case is too heavy?
active_learning: Keeping the whole journey running — desk, gate, cabin, landing — takes real focus and cooperation.
Children see the flight through from packing to arrival.
creating_thinking: Children invent destinations and the stories that go with them.
They solve problems in role — a lost passport, a delayed flight, a case that won't shut.
